articles.description:
In my previous article, we talked about why big databases (like Postgres or MySQL) act like a remote, slow mega-warehouse. Meanwhile, SQLite acts like a fast filing cabinet right under your desk.
But a common question arises: "Can a simple filing cabinet handle a serious, growing enterprise business?"
The answer is yes. You don't need a massive warehouse just because your business is growing. You just need to know how to organize your filing cabinet.
Here are the simple, practical tricks to make SQLite ready for enterprise apps.
By default, SQLite works like a cautious clerk: if someone is writing down a new file, nobody else can read the existing files until the writing is finished. This can cause a small delay.

articles.author: Ankit Maheshwari
articles.description:
Handling 10 inputs is easy. Handling 10 lakh inputs is where real skill shows. That's what time complexity measures.
It measures how the number of operations grows as input size grows — not seconds, not milliseconds.
function getFirst(arr) { return arr[0]; } // Always 1 step

function findMax(arr) {
  let max = arr[0];
  for (let i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) {
    if (arr[i] > max) max = arr[i];
  }
  return max;
}

Each step halves the problem. 1,000,000 elements → only ~20 steps. Example: Binary search.
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) { /* n×n ops */ }
}

articles.author: Rhumb
articles.description:
A URL tool can reach whatever the MCP server can reach.
If that server runs in a cloud, CI, laptop, VPC, or cluster, open fetch becomes a credential and internal-network boundary.
The safe default is to deny dangerous targets before the request leaves the runtime.
A fetch MCP server is not just a read tool. It is network egress running from wherever the agent host sits.
SSRF protection has to run before the HTTP request: parse the URL, resolve DNS, classify every resolved address, apply redirect policy, and deny metadata, loopback, private, IPv6 ULA, and in-cluster targets by default.
Allowing public URLs is not the same as allowing internal services. Internal fetch needs its own route card with caller, tenant, target, credential lane, quota owner, review owner, and receipt fields.
The pas…
articles.title: MCP Fetch SSRF Protection Checklist

Make Your REST API Callable by Claude: A Practical MCP Primer


Most APIs in 2026 still ship the same artifacts they shipped in 2016: an OpenAPI spec, a SwaggerUI page, maybe a Postman collection if the team is feeling generous. Those are great for humans. They are not enough for the thing that is actually consuming your API more and more often — an LLM running inside an editor or chat client.
If you want Claude, Cursor, Continue, or any other agent to call your API rather than just describe it, you need a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. This post explains what MCP is, why it's different from OpenAPI, and how to ship one without rewriting your backend.
An OpenAPI spec is a description: "here is POST /v1/customers, here are its fields, here are its responses." An agent reading OpenAP…
